title: Lemon meringue pie
summary: A tart, buttery lemon curd filling with a little gelatin for clean slices, under a tall meringue browned in the oven.
steps: Heat the oven to 175 °C (350 °F). Press the crust into a 23 cm (9 in) pie plate and bake 10–12 minutes. Leave the oven on.
Sprinkle the gelatin over the water and let it soften for 5 minutes.
In a heavy saucepan whisk the yolks, powdered erythritol, lemon juice and zest. Cook over low heat, whisking constantly, until thick enough to coat a spoon, about 8 minutes; do not let it boil.
Off the heat, whisk in the softened gelatin until it dissolves, then the butter a few cubes at a time. Pour into the crust.
Beat the egg whites with the cream of tartar to soft peaks. Add the powdered erythritol a spoonful at a time and beat to stiff, glossy peaks; beat in the vanilla.
Spread the meringue over the warm filling, sealing it right to the crust so it does not shrink. Swirl into peaks and bake 12–15 minutes, until the tips are golden.
Cool for an hour at room temperature, then refrigerate at least 3 hours before slicing with a wet knife.
dairy_free_notes: The crust is already dairy-free; with dairy-free butter the curd is a little less rich but sets just as well thanks to the gelatin.
tips: Erythritol meringue browns less than sugar meringue; a few seconds under the grill or a kitchen torch gives more colour.
Spread the meringue on warm filling: it cooks from below too and is less likely to weep.

origin.history: Lemon custards and lemon puddings in pastry were made in Britain and Europe for centuries, and meringue became common in European kitchens during the 1700s. The meringue-topped lemon pie familiar in America is often credited to the Philadelphia baker and cooking teacher Elizabeth Goodfellow in the early 1800s, though that attribution comes from later accounts.
